posts.name: Aaron Levie
posts.text:
The interesting thing about AI agents is that as a theoretical matter, their inference can kind of run anywhere. AI is one of the few areas of technology that isn’t *as* sensitive to latency back to the user. 

Long running agents are now going to be the norm, which means it’s ok to send off work to an AI factory somewhere and that work can essentially be largely done within that remote data center and a final result spit back to the user. The data can pass into these systems in an encrypted manner, be combed through by agents, and then disregarded right after. 

And because the economic value of the task is so high relative to the latency sensitivity (eg getting back $500 in value from an automated task, but it takes an extra second to return), you don’t have to have the inference to be particularly close to the user. 

Also, because inference is a temporary process with no sensitive data needing to be stored long term where the inference is happening, you can effectively treat AI factories as ephemeral systems, changing some of the data residency dynamics slightly.

Combined, this means you have more flexibility in where you can begin to deploy AI data centers. This is both a huge economic opportunity for the states or countries (or space) that want to take advantage of this fact. And it’s a loss to the states or countries that decide to forgo the opportunity.

To clarify again, the legal system does not allocate resources toward problems. In this context of holding back executive overreach, what the legal system does is rule whether executive or legislative actions are legal. Border security is an executive and legislative branch function.

The TGA isn’t the binding constraint (except in an inane legal sense you already know). The private sector resource base is. The govt monetizes that base by taxing it or issuing debt against it. Either way it needs a taxable resource base to run its balance sheet against. Without one you just get inflation. 

Now, you'll reply they don't need to tax it because they can issue money. But debt is just a claim on the same resource base the pvt sector already monetized when they created it. If you never tax it, the price level does the taxing for you when you create more money on the same resources.

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
Just remember: 

1. Every economic entity must fund its balance sheet. MMT misconstrues this concept by treating central government spending as self-funding because the sovereign issues the unit of account, but this ignores liability management: money creation injects liabilities into the private sector that alter asset prices, yield curves, and inflation expectations. Spending without credible funding mechanisms is not a free lunch; it is an inflation tax.

2. While loans create deposits endogenously, banks face strict liquidity and capital constraints. A bank must fund deposit outflows at clearing, manage reserves, and hold regulatory capital against risk-weighted assets. Credit expansion is constrained by balance sheet profitability and solvency risk, not an infinite creation tap.

3. Taxes don't just 'drive currency demand'; the real productive tax base defines a nation's fiscal space. A sovereign's ability to run persistent deficits depends entirely on an endogenous, highly productive private sector creating goods, services, and wealth to back that unit of account. Deficit capacity is a derivative of private-sector productivity, which is why the US can sustain deficits that developing economies like Somalia cannot.
 
4. The MMT claim that 'government deficits equal private financial surpluses' is an accounting truism, not an economic virtue. By definition, any borrower's liability is another party’s financial asset. Just as household borrowing creates financial assets for the non-household sector, government borrowing creates non-government assets. The critical question isn't whether the ledger balances, it always does, it's whether the debt fuels real output growth or simply inflates nominal claims against a fixed resource base. 

5. Real economic wealth is constrained by what the private sector produces. Since government *often* absorbs real resources (labor, capital, materials) rather than producing them, public spending redistributes or competes for private-sector output. Therefore, fiscal policy is bound by productive supply, and expanding nominal claims faster than real output inevitably degrades the currency. Private sector output constraints govt balance sheet expansion. See #3.

posts.text:
The recent drawdown in AI-capex-tied equities, and the open schadenfreude (as well as posts of remorse) that has accompanied it, got me thinking.

You are never as good as you think you are when you are winning, or as bad as you think you are when you are losing. The roll of the dice plays a far larger role in investment and life outcomes than most people care to admit.

Michael Mauboussin captures this dynamic brilliantly in *The Success Equation*, where he untangles the interplay of skill and luck across markets, sports, and business. His most counterintuitive insight is the “paradox of skill”: as any competitive field matures and the baseline level of talent, data, and analytical rigor rises, the gap between the best and the average participant narrows. Paradoxically, as skill becomes more uniform at the top, luck becomes a bigger determinant of the final outcome.

Nowhere is this clearer than in investing. At the institutional level, hundreds of smart, relentless analysts are parsing the same filings, tracking the same alternative data, and building similar models. When everyone at the table is highly capable, small exogenous variables—a sudden macro regime shift, an unexpected regulatory headline, or the exact timing of a liquidity squeeze—can turn a mediocre thesis into a windfall, or a rigorous, high-probability bet into a painful drawdown.

Looking backward, we hate randomness. We invent clean narratives about superior foresight during bull runs and fatal flaws during drawdowns so the uncertainty feels less threatening. Recognizing the true weight of luck doesn’t mean abandoning rigor—it means judging yourself by the quality of your process rather than the noise of a single outcome. It demands humility when your numbers look brilliant and resilience when the tape goes against you. Skill and effort matter enormously, and so does the roll of the dice. Both are true at once.

And my final advice - while it's a good idea to let your winners run, take profits along the way.  It's more important to live to fight another day.
